newsitem.title: UK: Treasuries cuddle thin range in London before data.
newsitem.headline: Treasuries cuddle thin range in London before data.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries stayed in a cosy range in London on Friday, awaiting the key payrolls data later which may give a hint on interest rates.
"It's just squeezing ahead. We haven't seen much trade, it's really in a range," said one trader at a Japanese bank in London.
By 1000 GMT, the long bond was quoted at 96-25 yielding 6.88 percent, unchanged from both Tokyo and the close in New York on Thursday.
Players have mostly positioned themselves according to whether the May payrolls figure will be convincingly strong for the U.S. Federal Reserve to pull the trigger on interest rates in July.

The data are due at 1230 GMT. A Reuters poll of economists forecast a rise of 219,000 in employment compared with a 142,000 rise previously. The unemployment rate was expected to rise to 5.0 percent, versus 4.9 percent in April. Average hourly earnings are expected to rise 0.4 percent compared with a 0.1 percent fall previously, while the average workweek was forecast to rise to 34.7 hours from 34.6 hours.
The consensus among traders was for a softer labour market, suggesting the Fed may leave interest rates alone again after its inaction last month.
But economists said the figures might not provide conclusive evidence on interest rates. In fact, they were more likely to point to a tightening.

"Overall the figures will still confirm that the economy is growing at a healthy pace. Wage pressures remain subdued and I don't think it's really going to provide sufficient information about interest rates," said Nick Stamenkovic, economist at DKB International in London.
"The evidence of a slowdown is still tentative and the market will be looking for more conclusive evidence before dismissing talk of any further rate hike," he said.
Economists said Treasuries would stay in a fairly narrow range even after the payrolls.
A low inflation outlook would attract investors to yields above seven percent, while yields were unlikely to fall decisively even if data gave concrete evidence of a slowdown, they said.
"If we saw a pickup in employment above 275,000, a strong rise in average earnings and an unchanged unemployment rate that would be the worst scenario. But I think that's unlikely," said Stamenkovic.
Strong payroll data could weigh heaviest on the short end of the U.S. curve, while the long end could be underpinned by a tame average earnings report.
The Fed would also be closely monitoring the unemployment rate, which in April fell to a 24-year low of 4.9 percent.
Meanwhile, Treasuries would continue to outperform their European counterparts until jitters over a single currency were removed, analysts said.
The September T-bond futures contract was one basis point higher at 110-01 in automated trade.
The 10-year bond outperformed on the spreads after market rumours that an upcoming auction may be cancelled. The 10-year/30-year spread widened to 28 basis points in London from Tokyo's 27.
